title: Properties and effects of atmospheric pollutants

notes.definition: Pollutants from burning fuels harm health and the environment: carbon monoxide is a toxic, colourless and odourless gas; sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems and acid rain; particulates cause global dimming and health problems.
explanation: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a toxic gas. It is colourless and odourless, so it is not easily detected by people. When it is breathed in, it combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells, so less oxygen can be carried around the body. This can cause drowsiness, headaches, unconsciousness and death. Faulty gas boilers and heaters with a poor air supply can produce carbon monoxide indoors, which is why carbon monoxide detectors are fitted in homes.
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) and oxides of nitrogen (NOₓ) cause respiratory problems in humans. They irritate the lungs and airways and can make conditions such as asthma worse.

Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen also cause acid rain. The gases dissolve in water droplets in clouds to form acidic solutions, which fall as acid rain. Acid rain damages trees and plants, makes lakes and rivers more acidic so that fish and other aquatic life are harmed, and reacts with and damages buildings and statues made of limestone or marble, as well as corroding metal structures.

Particulates are tiny solid particles, such as soot (carbon), and unburned hydrocarbons. They cause global dimming: particles in the atmosphere reflect sunlight back into space, so less sunlight reaches the Earth's surface. Particulates also cause health problems for humans, because very small particles can be breathed deep into the lungs, causing lung damage and making breathing and heart problems worse.

Exam questions often ask you to describe and explain problems caused by increased amounts of these pollutants. For each one, give the property or effect and explain why it matters, for example 'carbon monoxide is odourless so people do not notice it, and it reduces the oxygen carried by the blood'. You may also be asked to interpret data on pollution levels, such as the pH of rain or the concentration of a gas in ppm.
keyFacts: Carbon monoxide is toxic, colourless and odourless, so it is not easily detected.
Carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen carried in the blood.
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause respiratory problems.
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen cause acid rain.
Acid rain damages trees, acidifies lakes (harming fish) and damages limestone buildings and statues.
Particulates cause global dimming by reflecting sunlight.
Particulates cause health problems, especially lung damage.
Carbon monoxide detectors are used because people cannot smell or see the gas.

keyTerms.definition: Poisonous; harmful to living things even in small amounts.
CO, a toxic, colourless and odourless gas from incomplete combustion.
Rain made more acidic than normal by dissolved sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.
A reduction in the amount of sunlight reaching the Earth's surface, caused by particulates reflecting sunlight.
Illnesses of the lungs and airways, such as worsened asthma and bronchitis.
The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen; carbon monoxide combines with it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carbon monoxide can be smelled, like a gas leak.
misconceptions.right: In fact carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless, which is why it is so dangerous and why detectors are needed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think carbon dioxide is the main cause of acid rain.
misconceptions.right: In fact acid rain is mainly caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen; carbon dioxide makes rain only very slightly acidic.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think global dimming is the same as global warming.
misconceptions.right: In fact global dimming is a reduction in sunlight reaching the surface caused by particulates; global warming is caused by greenhouse gases.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think particulates only make things dirty.
misconceptions.right: In fact they cause serious health problems because tiny particles can be breathed deep into the lungs.

realWorld: Carbon monoxide detectors are recommended in homes with gas, oil or solid fuel appliances.
Limestone and marble buildings and gravestones in industrial cities show weathering from acid rain.
Low-emission zones in UK cities aim to reduce particulates and oxides of nitrogen from vehicles.
examTips: For carbon monoxide, give three properties: toxic, colourless and odourless, and explain that it is therefore not easily detected.
Learn the two effects of SO₂ and NOₓ: respiratory problems and acid rain.
Learn the two effects of particulates: global dimming and health problems.
Do not mix up pollutants: carbon dioxide is linked to climate change, not acid rain or toxicity in this topic.
summary: Carbon monoxide: toxic, colourless, odourless, not easily detected.
Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.
Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen: respiratory problems and acid rain.
Acid rain damages trees, lakes and limestone buildings.
Particulates: global dimming and health problems.

questions.question: Why is carbon monoxide difficult to detect?
options: It is only produced at night.
markScheme: 1 mark: colourless and odourless
questions.explanation: People cannot see or smell carbon monoxide, so they do not notice it.

questions.question: Which two pollutants cause acid rain?
options: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
markScheme: 1 mark: sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
questions.explanation: SO₂ and NOₓ dissolve in water in clouds to form acids.

questions.question: Which pollutant causes global dimming?
markScheme: 1 mark: particulates
questions.explanation: Particulates reflect sunlight, reducing the light reaching the ground.

questions.question: Which health problem is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen?
markScheme: 1 mark: respiratory problems
questions.explanation: These gases irritate the lungs and airways and can worsen asthma.

questions.question: How does carbon monoxide harm the human body?
options: It combines with haemoglobin, reducing the oxygen carried by the blood.
It causes acid rain inside the lungs.
It blocks sunlight from reaching the skin.
markScheme: 1 mark: combines with haemoglobin reducing oxygen carried
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, so less oxygen is transported.

questions.question: Which is an effect of acid rain?
markScheme: 1 mark: damage to limestone buildings
questions.explanation: Acids react with calcium carbonate in limestone and marble. Global dimming is caused by particulates.

questions.question: What is global dimming?
options: Clouds of carbon dioxide blocking the Moon
A reduction in sunlight reaching the Earth's surface caused by particulates
Darker nights caused by street lights
markScheme: 1 mark: less sunlight reaching the surface due to particulates
questions.explanation: Particles reflect sunlight back to space, dimming the light at the ground. The Sun itself is not changing.

questions.question: Why are particulates harmful to human health?
options: They can be breathed deep into the lungs and cause damage.
markScheme: 1 mark: breathed deep into the lungs and cause damage
questions.explanation: Very small particles penetrate deep into the lungs, causing lung and heart problems.

questions.question: Example data: the pH of rain in an area fell from 5.6 to 4.6. By what factor did the concentration of hydrogen ions increase?
markScheme: 1 mark: 10
questions.explanation: A decrease of 1 pH unit means the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of 10.

questions.question: Example data: in a city, particulate levels fell sharply after strict pollution controls. Which observation would most likely follow?
options: More sunlight reaching the ground and fewer breathing problems
markScheme: 1 mark: more sunlight reaching the ground and fewer breathing problems
questions.explanation: Fewer particulates means less global dimming and fewer health problems.

questions.question: Which pollutant from burning fuels is matched with its correct effect?
options: Sulfur dioxide: reduces oxygen carried by the blood
Oxides of nitrogen: respiratory problems and acid rain
markScheme: 1 mark: oxides of nitrogen: respiratory problems and acid rain
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide reduces oxygen carried by the blood; particulates cause global dimming; sulfur dioxide causes respiratory problems and acid rain.

questions.question: A carbon monoxide alarm sounds at 50 ppm. Convert 50 ppm into a percentage. (1% = 10 000 ppm)
questions.explanation: Divide ppm by 10 000 to get a percentage: 50 ÷ 10 000 = 0.005.

questions.question: Example data: the mean concentration of particulates in a city fell from 40 μg/m³ to 26 μg/m³. Calculate the percentage decrease.
markScheme: 1 mark: 35%

questions.question: Example data: in an area affected by particulates, the mean sunlight reaching the ground fell from 200 W/m² to 186 W/m². Calculate the percentage decrease.
markScheme: 1 mark: 7%
questions.explanation: Decrease = 14 W/m². 14 ÷ 200 = 0.07 = 7%. This is an example of global dimming.

questions.question:
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide released when 25 g of limestone (CaCO₃) reacts completely with sulfuric acid.
CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂
Mr: CaCO₃ = 100, CO₂ = 44
markScheme: 1 mark: moles CaCO₃ = 25 ÷ 100 = 0.25 mol
1 mark: 1 : 1 ratio so 0.25 mol CO₂
questions.explanation: The limestone is used up as the acid reacts with it, which is why statues and buildings are damaged.

questions.question: Example data: a room has a volume of 40 m³. A faulty heater releases carbon monoxide until its concentration is 0.01% by volume. Calculate the volume of carbon monoxide in the room in dm³. (1 m³ = 1000 dm³)
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.01% of 40 m³ = 0.004 m³
questions.explanation: 0.01 ÷ 100 × 40 = 0.004 m³. Multiply by 1000 to convert to dm³: 4 dm³. A small volume can still be dangerous because CO is toxic.

questions.question: Give three properties of carbon monoxide that make it dangerous.
markScheme: 1 mark: toxic (poisonous)
1 mark: colourless
1 mark: odourless
questions.explanation: Toxic makes it harmful; colourless and odourless mean it is not easily detected.

questions.question: Give two effects of particulates.
markScheme: 1 mark: global dimming
1 mark: health problems for humans (for example lung damage)
questions.explanation: These are the two effects named in the specification.

questions.question: Explain why homes with gas boilers should have carbon monoxide detectors.
markScheme: 1 mark: a faulty boiler or poor air supply can cause incomplete combustion producing carbon monoxide
1 mark: carbon monoxide is toxic but colourless and odourless, so people would not notice it without a detector
questions.explanation: Link source (incomplete combustion) to danger (toxic and undetectable).

questions.question: Describe how sulfur dioxide from a power station can lead to the death of fish in a lake.
markScheme: 1 mark: sulfur dioxide dissolves in water droplets in clouds to form acid rain
1 mark: acid rain makes the lake more acidic, which harms or kills fish
questions.explanation: Follow the chain: gas, dissolves, acid rain, acidic lake, fish harmed.

questions.question: Give two effects of acid rain on the environment or buildings.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: damages trees/plants; acidifies lakes and rivers, harming fish; damages limestone or marble buildings and statues; corrodes metal structures
questions.explanation: Acid rain affects living things and buildings.

questions.question: Explain why carbon monoxide poisoning can make a person drowsy and eventually unconscious.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin so the blood carries less oxygen
1 mark: so cells (especially in the brain) get less oxygen for respiration
questions.explanation: Less oxygen delivered means less aerobic respiration in cells, affecting the brain first.

questions.question: Suggest why global dimming might partly hide the warming effect of greenhouse gases.
markScheme: 1 mark: particulates reflect sunlight so less reaches the surface
1 mark: this has a cooling effect that partly cancels the warming caused by greenhouse gases
questions.explanation: The two effects act in opposite directions; reducing particulates may reveal more of the warming.

questions.question: State why a statue made of limestone becomes damaged in an area with acid rain.
markScheme: 1 mark: the acid reacts with the calcium carbonate in the limestone (so the stone wears away)
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with acids to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide, so the stone is slowly dissolved.

questions.question: Name the gas that combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen carried by the blood.
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide, not carbon dioxide, binds to haemoglobin.

questions.question: Describe the effects of sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen on humans and the environment.
markScheme: Indicative content: respiratory problems (irritate lungs, worsen asthma); dissolve in water droplets in clouds to form acid rain; acid rain damages trees and plants; acidifies lakes, harming fish; damages limestone or marble buildings and statues; corrodes metal.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): respiratory problems and acid rain described, with at least two effects of acid rain.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one effect named, for example 'acid rain'.
questions.explanation: Cover both human health and environmental effects for full marks.

questions.question:
A city council plans to ban older diesel vehicles from the city centre. Diesel engines release carbon monoxide, oxides of nitrogen, sulfur dioxide and particulates.
Explain the problems caused by each of these pollutants, and evaluate how the ban could benefit people and the environment.
markScheme: Indicative content: carbon monoxide: toxic, colourless and odourless so not easily detected; combines with haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carried; oxides of nitrogen and sulfur dioxide: respiratory problems such as asthma; dissolve in water in clouds to form acid rain, damaging trees, lakes (fish) and limestone buildings; particulates: health problems (lung damage, breathed deep into lungs) and global dimming. Evaluation: fewer vehicles means lower concentrations of these pollutants in the city centre, fewer respiratory problems, less damage to buildings; benefits mainly local; traffic may move elsewhere; other sources (power stations, heating) continue; conclusion: likely to improve air quality and health, especially for particulates and NOₓ.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): problems caused by all four pollutants explained correctly, with a reasoned evaluation of the ban including at least one limitation and a conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): problems caused by at least three pollutants described with some evaluation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some pollutants linked to simple effects with little evaluation.
questions.explanation: Explain each pollutant's effect first, then weigh up the benefits and limitations of the ban.
